title: Algorithms for railway crew management
contribution: An overview, co-signed by an FS planner, of how to model railway crew scheduling and rostering (set partitioning or arc models, chosen by where the feasibility rules live) and of the two Bologna codes for the FS competitions: the CFT Lagrangian set-covering heuristic (FASTER) and the assignment-based rostering bound and heuristic (FARO).
problem_entry: Industrial: deregulation pushes European railways to optimise, and FS instances (5,000 trips, up to 1,000,000 duties) dwarf airline ones; the two-phase decomposition is taken from practice and justified by depot returns, rules of different nature and what planners will accept, with the lost feedback between phases named (pp. 1, 3–4, 9).
key_idea: Choose the model by where the feasibility rules live (set partitioning for scheduling, arc model for rostering), then let dual information drive the heuristics: Lagrangian costs from several near-optimal multiplier vectors score a greedy with a priced core and fixing (CFT), and assignment-based bound increases score roster construction (pp. 8, 10–11, 16–17).
assumptions: Binary covering of graph nodes by circuits; pure SCP with free deadheading (covering, inclusion-maximal duties); FS rostering rules (6-day weeks, simple and double rests with a 40% share and a 58-hour average, 30-day and 7-day caps); arc costs on a 1440-minute lattice so that the bound is a whole number of days (pp. 6–9, 12–16).
proof_devices: SCP Lagrangian subproblem solved by the sign of each Lagrangian cost; subgradient s_i(u) = 1 − Σ_{j∈J_i} y_j(u) (p. 10)
v(RP) is always a whole number of days, so r bounds the number of weeks from below (p. 16)
LRP decomposes into an AP on the minimum of the three Lagrangian arc costs, a scalar search for the smallest integer r with αr ≥ λ1 r + λ2⌈0.4r⌉ + v(AP), and z = ⌈0.4r⌉; O(n³) (pp. 16–17)
two fixed multiplier pairs, (1440, 1440) and (1440, 0), give a tight bound v* from two APs (p. 17)
parametric O(n²) bound update per construction step of the roster heuristic (p. 17)
experiments: FASTER Table 1: seven FS SCPs up to 4,872 × 968,672 with subgradient LB, CFT value and the others' best, under 3,000 s on a PC 486/33 or 10,000 s on an HP 9000 735/125; CFT ties 4 and wins 3, never loses, 0.9% average gap (0.86% by my recomputation). FARO Table 2: eight instances of 21–525 duties with simple and Lagrangian bounds, weeks and Pentium 90 times; the text's count of 6 optimal out of 7 does not match the eight-row table, where 7 of 8 reach the bound within 1,185 s; the rows equal S017's post-competition results; single runs, no seeds (pp. 10–12, 18).
positioning: Surveys crew management, set covering (exact codes ruled out by size; the Lagrangian line from Balas and Ho; greedy fast but weak) and rostering literature; railways set against airlines by size and transit by objective; CFT said to outperform published methods; details deferred to the authors' reports (pp. 2, 4, 9–10, 12).
writing: An outline presenting the techniques as those currently adopted at FS; modelling advice framed as experience; firm verdicts; a toy roster figure explains the crew count; no conclusions section; paragraphs shared nearly verbatim with S003 and S017 (pp. 1–4, 8, 10–11, 17–18).
limits_future: Decomposition is a compromise and phase feedback only suggested; the core definition is critical; exact SCP is out of reach at FS size; unstated: anonymous rivals and a summary count that does not match its table; the refinement is described differently from S017's final version; no future work (pp. 4, 9, 11, 17–18).

title: Modeling and solving the crew rostering problem
contribution: A general crew-rostering model as looped cycles in a three-arc-type multigraph, a Lagrangian bound computed by two assignment problems, and a bound-driven constructive heuristic with bound-guided refinement: the FORTRAN code that won the FS/AIRO FARO competition of 1995.
problem_entry: A competition (FS and AIRO, 1994: three instances of up to 1,000 duties, 90 minutes on a PC 486/33) and a gap in objective: earlier rostering work balances workload in urban transit, whereas railways minimise crews under more involved sequencing rules (pp. 2–4).
key_idea: Encode the sequencing rules in arc lengths, drop the infeasible-path constraints and relax the two rest-count constraints so that the bound is one AP on the cheapest Lagrangian arc per pair, with multipliers fixed by the 1440-minute lattice; build rosters one at a time by parametric bound increases on zero reduced-cost arcs, and refine by removing the rosters whose imposition raises the bound (pp. 6–16).
assumptions: Periodic rostering in integer minutes; weeks of k days with rest types, shares and caps; FARO rules (k = 6, q = 60, β = 0.4, 58-hour average rest, 30-day and 7-day caps, an optional special roster, a hierarchical objective); arc lengths differing by multiples of 1440; lower-level bounds valid only when the higher-level ones are tight (pp. 4–6, 12–13, 17–20).
proof_devices: validity of the relaxed weeks inequality (15) by comparing its right-hand side with that of (9) on feasible solutions (p. 11)
Proposition 1: keep the cheapest Lagrangian arc per pair, solve one AP, take the smallest integer w satisfying (16) and set z := ⌈βw⌉; O(n³) (p. 12)
counting variables and inequalities (9)–(13), redundant in the full ILP, added because they survive the relaxation (p. 10)
trivial O(n) bounds from each cap, e.g. paid time, and FARO's five bounds with their special-roster versions (pp. 11, 19)
ε added to every direct arc that needs a technical interval yields a technical-interval bound, valid only when the weeks bound is tight (p. 20)
a dummy duty of three idle days forces the special roster: LB′, min{LB, LB′} and rules (18)–(19) (pp. 20–21)
parametric AP re-solves: O(n²) per step and per roster, O(n³) overall (pp. 13–16)
experiments: Competition Table 1 (FARO164, FARO360, FARO525: BO 48, 112, 165 weeks against bounds 48, 108, 164; NA and TO worse; three of seven teams produced valid solutions) and Table 3 for the post-competition final version on 36 instances (8 FARO plus 28 merged pairs; 60- and 150-minute limits; Pentium 90): claims of 26 of 36 at the bound and a 0.8% gap; my recount gives 25 within the limits (26 with a separate 300-minute run), 0.69% over all rows (0.78% over the merged ones), a misnamed instance in the text and one time above its stated limit; the abstract's real-world instances of up to 1,000 duties fit only the merged ones (at most 911), the FS instances having at most 525; no rival on the 36, single runs (pp. 2, 22–25).
positioning: Prior rostering, airline set-partitioning and cyclic-scheduling work listed in one paragraph and set aside by objective; rival teams named with their reports; the competition call and jury minutes cited (pp. 3, 22, 24, 26).
writing: The abstract runs gap, model, AP bound, heuristic, results and competition win; design choices justified by experience; the general model kept apart from the FARO specifics; firm verdicts; no conclusions section (pp. 2, 4–21, 23–24).
limits_future: LP strengthening of the path constraints declined; the bound is weak where paid time binds (FARO360, confirmed by relaxing that constraint); trivial bounds are blind to technical intervals; hierarchical bounds are conditional; no future work (pp. 9, 20, 22).

title: Algorithms for the set covering problem
contribution: A computational survey of SCP relaxations, heuristics and exact methods on the OR-Library classes A–H by the authors of the leading heuristic, with a new exact LP code that beats CPLEX 4.0.8's LP algorithms on every instance and the finding that CPLEX and MINTO compete with special-purpose exact codes and gain from the authors' preprocessing.
problem_entry: SCP as the model behind railway and transit crew scheduling; the scope is fixed by one public test bed (methods never tried on the OR Library are not described; the easy classes 4, 5, 6 and e are dropped) and the state of the art is stated in instance sizes (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: The best SCP methods all rest on the LP relaxation, solved exactly or heuristically in its dual by Lagrangian or surrogate multipliers; relaxations used inside heuristics are judged by the solutions they drive, not by their bounds (pp. 2–5).
assumptions: Pure SCP with positive integer costs and q nonzeros; reduction rules recalled but left out per algorithm; OR-Library classes A–H (300 × 3,000 to 1,000 × 10,000, densities 2–20%, costs 1–100); the integrality property of the Lagrangian subproblem (pp. 1–3; Table 1, p. 12).
proof_devices: integrality property of the Lagrangian subproblem: the Lagrangian dual equals the LP dual (p. 3)
greedy repair of any multiplier vector into a dual-feasible one without lowering the bound (p. 3)
Lagrangian cost fixing in both directions against UB, with ≥ (p. 4)
Balas–Carrera partial relaxation over disjoint rows: O(q) per subproblem, best bound equal to the LP value (p. 4)
optimal removal of redundant columns as an SCP of its own (p. 6)
explanatory argument: bounds markedly stronger than the LP are very hard to get cheaply, so LP-based branch-and-bound and general-purpose ILP packages win (p. 8)
experiments: Table 1 (40 instances): the authors' LP code (10.25 s on average, 6.54 s of it inside CPLEX) against CPLEX 4.0.8 primal, dual, network and barrier (419, 46, 46 and 370 s), faster than dual and network on every instance (my recomputation: ratio of averages about 4.45, stated as almost 5); Tables 2–4, not in this copy, summarised in the prose: heuristics on A–D and E–H, and exact codes against CPLEX 4.0.8 and MINTO 2.3 on the plain instances (about 700 and 750 s) and with the authors' preprocessing (about 400 and 500 s); DECstation 5000/240 times, rivals converted with Dongarra's figures, one value per method (pp. 2, 5, 7–9, 12).
positioning: History deferred to Balas and to Ceria, Nobili and Sassano; methods described in their authors' terms with gaps named and one critique of Beasley's LP use; the authors' codes are best or tied throughout; general-purpose solvers presented as competitive (pp. 1, 5–9).
writing: Relaxations, heuristics and exact methods, each closed by a comparison; few explicit hedges; approximate averages, with the LP speed-up rounded up; paragraphs reused from S012; no conclusions section, ending on the sentence about general-purpose solvers (pp. 2–9).
limits_future: Rival times converted crudely; some comparisons impossible; preprocessing details omitted; Tables 2–4 absent from this copy; no future work (pp. 2, 8).

coauthors: Alberto Caprara, Paolo Toth (DEIS Bologna); Fischetti at DEI, University of Padova

quotes.text: According to our opinion, this is not a drawback within heuristic algorithms, where the main objective is to determine good SCP solutions without insisting in proving optimality.

This shows that the state-of-the-art general-purpose ILP solvers are competitive with the best exact algorithms for SCP presented in the literature, and that their performance can sensibly be improved by an external preprocessing procedure.
